title: TF module upgrade resilience and runtime chaos checklist
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, pragmatic playbook for TF module upgrades and the most common runtime failures we see in VPC/on-prem installs. Designed to be used during canaries and fast post-upgrade triage. Focus on quick hypotheses, measurable smoke-tests, and safe rollback/mitigation actions.

Scope:
- Applies to: Terraform module upgrades that change runtime images, kernel/kernel-module picks, volumes, or node boot config in private deployments (VPC + on-prem).
- Not covered: full network redesigns or customer-specific custom modules (those need a separate runbook).

High-level triage (one-liner):
1) Identify failure surface (control-plane vs runtime vs infra).
2) Run the "fast health" smoke tests below.
3) Map failing tests to hypotheses and run the targeted checks.
4) If canary is unhealthy and root cause unknown after 15–30m, rollback to previous TF state and escalate.

Fast-health smoke tests (run on canary cluster/node):
- API reachability: curl -sSf -m 5 https://<ingress-ip>/healthz -> expect 200 and JSON {"ok":true}
- Runtime readiness: kubectl -n redwood get pods -l app=redwood-runtime -o wide -> expect pods in Ready state and 1/1 containers
- Inference smoke: curl -sS -X POST https://<ingress-ip>/v1/generate -d '"{\"prompt\":\"small test\" }"' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -> expect 200 + tokens returned within SLA
- KV-cache sanity: curl -sS https://<ingress-ip>/internal/kvcache/stats -> expect hit_ratio > 0 or known safe value (if cache disabled expect 0)
- Disk pressure: ssh node 'df -h /var/lib/redwood' -> expect >10% free
- GPU health: ssh node 'nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.free --format=csv,noheader' -> expect free > 200MB (varies by model)

Hypotheses & targeted checks (fast mapping):
1) Networking / MTU / CNI regressions -> checks:
   - curl from ingress to control-plane and node IPs, traceroute/mtr to dependency endpoints.
   - check kube-proxy logs, CNI plugin (calico/flannel) logs: kubectl -n kube-system logs -l k8s-app=calico-node
   - dmesg grep for skb/XDP errors on nodes.

2) Terraform state drift / provider version mismatch -> checks:
   - terraform plan -var-file=secrets.tfvars; compare resource diffs.
   - terraform state list | grep module.runtime -> ensure expected resources exist.
   - check provider versions: cat .terraform.lock.hcl or terraform providers lock; look for major provider bumps.

3) Runtime binary / kernel / driver ABI mismatch (most common on on-prem GPUs) -> checks:
   - ssh node 'uname -r && cat /etc/os-release'
   - ssh node 'lsmod | egrep "nvidia|nv_peer_mem|nvidia_uvm"'
   - docker/k8s container logs for libc/torch import errors (GLIBCXX, CUDNN mismatches).
   - runtime pod log grep: kubectl -n redwood logs <pod> | tail -n 200 | egrep -i "cuda|cudnn|libc|segfault|undefined symbol"

4) KV-cache corruption or incompatible format after upgrade -> checks:
   - size check: ssh node 'du -sh /var/lib/redwood/kvcache'
   - service exposed stats: /internal/kvcache/stats -> check last_compact_time and errors.
   - runtime logs contain 'kvcache' error stack traces.

5) Disk pressure / inode exhaustion -> checks:
   - df -i to check inode usage, journalctl for OOM/kernel logs, ls -lah /var/log/redwood to spot huge files.

Quick commands / expected outputs (copy-paste friendly):
- API health:
  curl -sSf -m 5 https://$INGRESS/healthz || echo "HEALTH FAIL"
- Pod health:
  kubectl -n redwood get pods -l app=redwood-runtime -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}: {.status.phase} {.status.containerStatuses[0].ready}
{end}'
- Tail runtime errors:
  kubectl -n redwood logs -f $(kubectl -n redwood get pods -l app=redwood-runtime -o name | head -1)
- Disk quick check:
  ssh $NODE "df -h /var/lib/redwood && df -i /var/lib/redwood"
- GPU quick check:
  ssh $NODE "nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.free --format=csv,noheader"

Terraform-focused pre-upgrade checklist (short):
- Pin provider versions in lockfile and verify no major bumps since last release.
- Run terraform plan with the exact state backend lock (avoid concurrent applies).
- Run a dry-run of module upgrades in a small staging cluster that mirrors node images and driver versions.
- Add targeted destroy/create plan for cgroup/kernel boot flags changes to avoid simultaneous mass reboot.
- Create upgrade window and lock team pager rotations.

Canary rollout sequence (recommended):
1) Apply infra-only changes (disks/volumes, networking) -> validate.
2) Apply control-plane changes (ingress/route) -> validate.
3) Apply runtime module changes to a single canary node/device -> validate smoke tests.
4) If canary passes for N minutes (15–60), ramp to 10% then 50% then 100%.

Rollback procedures (fast):
- If TF change is small (image tag or deployment change): terraform apply -var-file=previous.tfvars -target=module.runtime --auto-approve
- If TF state must be reverted to prior statefile snapshot: restore state from backups (s3/gs) and run terraform apply against restored state.
- For Kubernetes: kubectl rollout undo deployment/redwood-runtime -n redwood --to-revision=<previous>
- If runtime binary crash: systemctl restart redwood-runtime OR kubectl delete pod <pod> to force re-schedule.

Fast mitigations (one-liners):
- Disable cache to get services healthy (temporary): kubectl -n redwood set env deployment/redwood-runtime REDWOOD_KV_CACHE_ENABLED=false
- Scale down heavy workers to stop overload:
  kubectl -n redwood scale deploy redwood-worker --replicas=1
- Free space on node by rotating logs (careful): ssh $NODE 'sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=2d'

Observability queries (prometheus / grafana examples):
- request latency P95: rate(redwood_runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]) -> summarize by le buckets to get P95
- error rate: increase(redwood_runtime_errors_total[5m]) / increase(redwood_runtime_requests_total[5m])
- kv cache hit ratio: sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total[5m])) / (sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total[5m])) + sum(rate(kv_cache_misses_total[5m])))
- GPU memory pressure: max_over_time(gpu_memory_used_bytes[5m]) / max_over_time(gpu_memory_total_bytes[5m])
- node disk free: node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/var/lib/redwood"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/var/lib/redwood"}

KV-cache corruption runbook (short):
1) Identify corruption: repeated 'kvcache: invalid header' or constant compaction errors in logs.
2) Immediately set runtime to read-only cache mode: set REDWOOD_KV_CACHE_ENABLED=false.
3) Export/backup existing cache directory: tar czf /tmp/kvcache-backup-$(date +%s).tgz /var/lib/redwood/kvcache
4) Rotate cache: rename /var/lib/redwood/kvcache -> /var/lib/redwood/kvcache-corrupt-<ts>
5) Restart runtime and run preheat script to re-warm cache (we use small corpus smoke prompts).
6) If data-latency unacceptable, restore from prebuilt cache artifacts (if available) or roll back runtime image.

Common failure fingerprints and immediate action mapping:
- "GLIBCXX_3.4.x not found" -> driver / binary ABI mismatch -> rollback runtime to previous working image + check system libc versions.
- OOMKill of runtime process -> scale down concurrency or increase node memory; check cgroups and kube OOM events.
- Permission denied writing to volume -> check SELinux/AppArmor changes, verify mountOptions from TF module.
- NFS stale file handle / i/o errors -> cordon node, restart nfs client, failover to replica if available.

Postmortem and follow-up (minimal template):
- Summary: one-line impact and timeline.
- Root cause hypotheses tested and evidence.
- Actions taken (short) and rollback time.
- Long-term mitigations (changes to TF, monitoring, pre-flight tests).
- Owners for follow-ups and ETA.

Notes / pro-tips:
- Avoid mass node reboots in one batch; stagger with a delay equal to typical pod restart + health-check interval.
- Keep a small, pinned staging cluster with the oldest supported OS/driver combos we still serve; use for upgrade rehearsals.
- Use a canned set of 10 prompts that exercise: small, long, streaming, and high-memory generation to surface subtle regressions.
- When in doubt, flip to canary-only and escalate to eng-telemetry + runtime owners.

Appendix: helpful quick links and commands:
- Terraform state inspect: terraform state show module.runtime.redwood_deployment[0]
- Snapshot and restore state: aws s3 cp s3://tf-state-backups/backup-<ts>.tfstate ./terraform.tfstate && terraform apply -auto-approve
- Quick log aggregator (remote): ssh $BASTION 'journalctl -u kubelet -f' (follow combined with `kubectl logs -n redwood -l app=redwood-runtime -c runtime --tail=200 -f`)

End of playbook. Keep a copy near upgrade windows and attach to PRs that change runtime or node-level resources.
